summary: Allows transaction-level authentication of DNS messages using shared secrets and one-way hashing. It can authenticate dynamic updates as coming from an approved client, or responses as coming from an approved name server. It is on the standards track and was replaced by RFC 8945.

plainLanguage.summary: Two DNS servers share a secret word. Each message gets a stamp made from that word, so the other side can tell it is real and was not changed.

questions: how does tsig authenticate dns messages
what is the tsig fudge value
subtitle: A lightweight way for DNS clients and servers to authenticate each message with a shared secret and a keyed hash.

tldr.problem: Public key DNS security is computationally expensive and complex, which is impractical for simple stub resolvers and for authenticating dynamic updates and zone transfers.
tldr.mechanism: Two parties share a secret key. Each DNS message gets a TSIG record holding an HMAC-MD5 digest over the message and some timing data, so the receiver can check who sent it and that it was not altered.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2845 has been obsoleted by RFC 8945. It did not specify how to distribute the shared secrets.

today: RFC 2845 has been obsoleted by RFC 8945. It was updated by RFC 3645, RFC 4635 and RFC 6895, and it updates RFC 1035.

sections.title: Why TSIG Exists
sections.content:
DNS had been extended in RFC 2535 with public key signatures. Those need caching of keys and tracing through chains of signatures, which is impractical for simple "stub" resolvers that have no cache and depend on a caching server. Public key transaction signatures are also very expensive to compute.

This RFC instead uses a message authentication code, specifically HMAC-MD5, a keyed hash function, to give an efficient point-to-point way to authenticate and check the integrity of transactions. The same mechanism can authenticate dynamic update requests ([RFC2136]) as a lightweight alternative to RFC 2137, and can protect zone transfers, including glue records.

The scheme relies on shared secret keys, which must be protected like private keys. The RFC says it is unsuitable for general server to server authentication among servers that talk to many others, because the number of shared keys grows quadratically. It suits resolvers on hosts that talk to only a few recursive servers, and forwarders talking to a small number of preconfigured upstream servers.
sections.plainLanguage: The big, fancy way of proving who you are takes too much work for small helpers. This is a quick way: if you and one other person share a secret, you can prove who you are cheaply.

sections.title: The TSIG Record
sections.content:
TSIG is a new record type with type code 250. It is a meta-record that MUST NOT be cached: it is computed for one DNS transaction and discarded once it has authenticated a message. The record NAME is the name of the key, in domain name syntax, and should uniquely identify the key among keys the two hosts may share. The CLASS is ANY and the TTL is 0.

The RDATA carries the algorithm name, the time signed (a 48-bit count of seconds since 1 January 1970 UTC), a fudge (the seconds of error permitted in the time), the MAC size and MAC, the original message ID, an error code and optional other data. HMAC-MD5 is the only algorithm specified and is mandatory to implement. New algorithm names must be registered with IANA, and all multi-octet integers are in network byte order.
sections.plainLanguage: The stamp is a small extra note attached to the message. It says which secret was used, when it was stamped, how much clock difference is allowed, and holds the stamp itself.

sections.title: Signing and Checking Messages
sections.content:
To send a signed message, the sender builds the message, computes the keyed digest and appends the TSIG record to the additional data section, incrementing the ARCOUNT. If the TSIG does not fit without truncating, the server must instead send a response that has only the question and a TSIG, with the TC bit set and RCODE 0, and the client SHOULD retry over TCP.

The digest covers the whole DNS message in wire format as it was before the TSIG was added, plus selected TSIG variables: the key name, class, TTL, algorithm name, time signed, fudge, error and other data. The RDLEN and MAC size are not included. The time signed and fudge are included to defend against replay attacks, because otherwise an attacker could replay old messages with refreshed times. When a server signs a response, the digest also includes the request MAC, tying the answer to the question. A server must not sign a response to an unsigned request.

On receipt, a TSIG must be the last record in the additional section; multiple TSIGs are not allowed, and otherwise the packet is dropped with RCODE 1 (FORMERR). The server checks, in order, the key, the time values and the MAC.

For a TCP session with many DNS envelopes, such as a zone transfer, the TSIG MUST be on the first and last envelopes and on at least every 100th envelope, each later one covering a running prior digest. If a client's check fails it MUST close the connection.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender mixes the message and the secret to make a stamp. The receiver mixes the same things and checks the stamps match. The reply's stamp also includes the stamp from the question, so the answer proves it belongs to that question.

sections.title: Errors and Clock Checks
sections.content:
The server checks the key first. An unknown key produces an unsigned response with RCODE 9 (NOTAUTH) and TSIG error 17 (BADKEY). Next it checks the time: if the server time is outside Time Signed plus or minus the fudge, it responds with NOTAUTH and error 18 (BADTIME). That response is signed and carries the server's current time in the other data field, so the client can verify it without hitting another time error. Finally, a MAC that fails to verify gets NOTAUTH and error 16 (BADSIG), unsigned. The server SHOULD log each error, while taking care that logging does not open a denial of service.

The client discards responses that lack an expected TSIG or fail to validate, unless the RCODE is 9, in which case it tries to verify the response as an error response. A time error means the clocks are not synchronized; resolvers MUST NOT adjust their clocks based on BADTIME errors. After a MAC error the client may retry, but trying a different shared key is better.

A forwarding server that shares no secret with the originator MUST forward a TSIG unchanged. If it does share one, it processes it and, if possible, adds its own TSIG, and clears the AD flag when no transaction security is available onward.
sections.plainLanguage: If the stamp is wrong, the message is turned away and the sender is told why: wrong secret, wrong time, or a stamp that does not match. If the clocks disagree the receiver tells the sender what time it thinks it is.

sections.title: Handling the Shared Secrets
sections.content:
The RFC makes no provision for distributing secrets. It expects an administrator to configure servers and clients out of band, for example by "sneaker-net", until a secure automated key distribution mechanism exists.

Secrets are very sensitive and every available step should be taken to protect them. Hosts that store them generally need physical protection, and on multi-user machines unprivileged users must have no access. Because resolvers often run unprivileged and name servers privileged, the RFC suggests a host using transaction authentication should probably have a stub resolver plus a local caching and forwarding name server. Strong random secrets are essential, and a secret should be at least as long as the digest: 16 bytes for HMAC-MD5 or 20 bytes for HMAC-SHA1.
sections.plainLanguage: The secret is like a house key. The document does not say how to hand keys out. It only says to keep them safe, make them hard to guess and never leave them lying around.

sections.title: Security Considerations and IANA
sections.content:
The scheme is much cheaper than public key signatures and gives strong authentication for the last hop from a local name server to the user resolver, as long as the secret stays secret. Secrets should be changed periodically, never sent in the clear, and never shared by more than two entities. If a client host is compromised, the server should suspend all secrets known to it.

TSIG does not authenticate the original source data, only its transmission between two parties who share a secret. A compromised zone master could still supply bad data, unless the server also performs the full RFC 2535 checks. The fudge value is a trade-off: too large risks replay attacks, too small causes failures when clocks differ or the network is slow. The recommended value in most situations is 300 seconds.

IANA is expected to maintain registries of algorithm names, starting with HMAC-MD5.SIG-ALG.REG.INT, and of TSIG error values, with new entries under the IETF Consensus policy.
sections.plainLanguage: The stamp proves a message came from your friend, not that the message is true. A good fudge is like allowing a few minutes of clock difference: too much lets cheats reuse old notes, too little rejects honest ones.
